sharedText: the sixteenth year of the reign
reason: The same serial-counting coincidence set out at Alma 28:7: the Book of Mormon dates continuously by the year of the reign of the judges and must produce every ordinal in turn, so a match with the KJV's regnal dates carries nothing. The formula itself is first used at Alma 1:1.

'Why do ye yoke yourselves with such foolish things' invites Acts 15:10's 'to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples' and Galatians 5:1's 'yoke of bondage' — Galatians 5:1 is already adjudicated at Mosiah 21:13 and 23:13 — and the invitation is strengthened by Korihor's bondage rhetoric at 30:24 and 30:27. It will not carry a link: only the noun is shared, the Book of Mormon reflexivises the verb in a way no KJV verse does, and the metaphor of a yoke for religious obligation is common to every English writer of the period. The verse's real dependence is on Hebrews 11:1, filed at 30:15.

Alma 30:18 and 30:23 both use 'lift up their heads', and the KJV's memorable instance is Luke 21:28, 'then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh' — an eschatological summons. The sense here is opposed twice over: at 30:18 the heads are lifted 'in their wickedness', and at 30:23 lifting them is what Korihor says the priests prevent. Psalm 24:7's lifted gates are further off still. The idiom is ordinary and the parallel is an artifact of it.

sharedText: labour, working with our own hands
reason: 'I have labored ... with mine own hands, for my support' is the phrase adjudicated in this book at Alma 1:3, where Nehor's denial of it is argued in full, and at Mosiah 18:24 and 27:5 before that. Within a book a repeat is recorded rather than relinked (ADJUDICATING §4), and the argument is at Alma 1:3. What is new at Alma 30:32 is not the phrase but the frame around it — the whole of 1 Thessalonians 2:5-9's defence against the charge of preaching for gain — and the link is filed there.

'What evidence have ye that there is no God' is the third of the chapter's three contacts with Hebrews 11:1, and the sharpest, since 'evidence' in the sense of grounds for belief occurs in exactly one KJV verse and this is Alma using it back at Korihor. It is adjudicated with the other two at 30:15, where the whole exchange across verses 13, 15 and 40 is set out; a reader arriving here is sent there.

sharedText: the heavens declare the glory of God
reason: Alma's argument from the motion of the planets — 'all things denote there is a God ... and also all the planets which move in their regular form, doth witness that there is a Supreme Creator' — is the classical argument from design, and Psalm 19:1 and Romans 1:20 are the KJV verses that state it. Neither is verbally present: no word beyond 'God' is shared with Psalm 19:1, and Romans 1:20's 'the invisible things of him ... are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made' is already adjudicated at 2 Nephi 6:3. The passage's actual source is Acts 17, where the same argument answers the same charge about an unknown God, and the link is filed at 30:28.

Matthew 12:39 and 16:4 ('an evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign') are the KJV's judgment on sign-seeking and stand behind this whole exchange; Matthew 16:4 is adjudicated at Mosiah 1:13. The verse that supplies the Book of Mormon's actual sentence is John 4:48, 'Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe', which Korihor reproduces in the first person at 30:48, and the link is filed there with Matthew 12:39 as a composite.

'Went about from house to house, a begging for his food' looks like the imprecation of Psalm 109:10, 'let his children be continually vagabonds, and beg', and 'from house to house' occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Luke 10:7, Acts 2:46, Acts 20:20, 1 Timothy 5:13). None of the four is about begging and none has any other contact here. The source of the detail is Acts 13:11, where the stricken Elymas 'went about seeking some to lead him by the hand' — a KJV singleton — and it is catalogued with the rest of the Elymas sequence at 30:22. Note that the 1830's 'a begging' is a dialect participle the 1920 edition removed; it is not KJV.

'Doth speedily drag them down to hell' is close in sense to 2 Peter 2:4's 'cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness', and 2 Peter 2 is genuinely behind this chapter's portrait of Korihor — the link at 30:31 says so. But the verb here is 'drag', which is in no KJV verse, and no run is shared. Registered rather than passed over because the epistle's presence elsewhere in the chapter makes the parallel tempting.
